body.text: In short:
A sample of discoloured water from a Sandy Bay home has tested above guideline levels for lead and manganese.
TasWater had previously told a resident the water was "safe to drink".
What's next?
Health authorities say harm is unlikely from limited consumption, though TasWater is reviewing its messaging.
Testing of viscous, orange water that Tasmania's water authority had told a customer was safe to drink has returned levels of heavy metals above drinking water guidelines.
Two weeks ago, Sandy Bay resident Emma Thornley turned the taps on in her house and found discoloured water coming out. It happened throughout the day.
A load of white clothing came out of the washing machine with dark orange stains while thick, orange water poured from the kitchen tap.

State water provider, TasWater, advised residents in the area at the time that emergency repairs were being carried out on a nearby burst water main, and that drinking water "may be discoloured and cloudy" but was "safe to drink".
Ms Thornley called TasWater to tell the authority her water did not appear safe to drink so that it could notify other customers.
She said her concerns were dismissed.
"I actually asked her to guarantee on the recorded line if this water was safe and would not contain anything harmful like heavy metals," she said.
"They were very quick to respond that it was absolutely safe to drink and there would be no heavy metals or contaminants in it.
"The words they used were that this was the normal water you drink every day; it's just got some sediment in it."
Ms Thornley paid to have the water tested at Analytical Services Tasmania, which is part of the state's Department of Natural Resources and Environment.
The sample was not large enough to test for mercury but was tested for lead and manganese.
It found 25 micrograms of lead and 3,210 micrograms (3.21 milligrams) of manganese per litre.

According to the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG), the highest acceptable concentration for lead is 5 micrograms per litre of drinking water, while for manganese it is 100 micrograms (0.1 milligram) per litre.
"I now have lots of questions about why TasWater continued telling me that this was safe to drink," Ms Thornley said.

"It also makes me question, in the past when we've had discoloured water, and we've contacted them and told them and the general response is just 'flush the taps if you're worried' and 'it's totally safe to drink', was it actually safe to drink?"
TasWater will review 'incorrect' messaging
The results of the testing prompted Analytical Services Tasmania to notify Public Health and Tasmania's drinking water officer, Cameron Dalgleish.
Mr Dalgleish wrote to Ms Thornley on November 11 and said he had spoken to TasWater about the issue.
"They have undertaken to do a full review around the incomplete (and incorrect) messaging and their response to the emergency works," Mr Dalgleish wrote.
"TasWater and I have agreed to reword any advice given out in these situations."
Mr Dalgleish said he had also flagged questions about the customer service response with the Tasmanian Economic Regulator.
Resident wants more transparency about testing

Living in a suburb with aging water infrastructure, Ms Thornley said she had received several text message notifications from TasWater in the past two years, advising customers to run their taps and saying the water may be discoloured but was safe to drink.
On other occasions, the water had come out cloudy, but she did not receive any communication from TasWater.
Ms Thornley wants to see more transparency about TasWater's testing processes, saying there needs to be more accurate communication to its customers.
"If there are times where it is not safe to drink then I want to be notified and I want TasWater to come up with a plan for people,"
she said.
TasWater did not take water samples directly from the affected area at the time.

The utility's general manager of customer and community, Callan Paske, said TasWater had advised customers via text message on the day of the emergency works to run their outside tap until clear to remove sediment or cloudiness, as per its standard practice.
TasWater's investigation into the incident is continuing.
"We are working closely with the Department of Health to review water quality following the outage and our ongoing communications procedures,"
Mr Paske said.
Health impacts unlikely, department says
Mr Paske said TasWater had since done additional testing within the Sandy Bay drinking water network, which showed the water met Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and was safe to drink.
"We conduct more than 330,000 water quality tests across our network each year to support our commitment to providing safe and reliable drinking water," he said.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health said that health harms from limited consumption of the water on the day were unlikely.
"ADWG values are designed to protect health over a lifetime of consuming drinking water," they said.
"While water that exceeds ADWG values does not meet drinking water standards, a single or short-term exceedance does not necessarily mean that health harms will occur."
Mr Paske said anyone with concerns about the appearance, taste or quality of their drinking water should contact TasWater.
